subject: Philosophy
title: 1. Definition, Nature and Scope of Philosophy

segments.text: Philosophy is disciplined critical inquiry into basic questions about reality, knowledge, value, reasoning and human life.

Its branches commonly include metaphysics/ontology, epistemology, ethics, logic, political philosophy and philosophy of mind/language. Philosophy differs from mere opinion because it asks for reasons, coherence and examination of assumptions.

Philosophy is disciplined inquiry into fundamental questions about reality, knowledge, value, reasoning, mind, language and political life. The traditional phrase “love of wisdom” explains the word’s origin but not the method. Philosophers build arguments, examine concepts, test assumptions, distinguish meanings and ask what reasons support a conclusion.

Philosophy differs from mere opinion because a philosophical claim must be defended by reasons open to criticism. It differs from empirical science in method, although many philosophical questions interact closely with scientific findings.

Metaphysics or ontology asks what exists and what kinds of things are real. Epistemology asks what knowledge is and how belief can be justified. Ethics asks what makes actions, character or institutions right or good. Logic studies valid reasoning. Political philosophy studies authority, justice, liberty and obligation. Philosophy of mind, language, science and religion apply philosophical analysis to specific domains.
These branches overlap. A debate about free will, for example, involves metaphysics, philosophy of mind, moral responsibility and sometimes law.

blocks.text: How to read a philosophical text

segments.text: Identify the question, the conclusion, the reasons offered for it, hidden assumptions, objections and possible replies. A thinker’s famous sentence is less important than the argument that gives it meaning.

In examination writing, reconstruct the position fairly before criticizing it. The strongest criticism targets a specific premise, inference or implication rather than calling a philosophy “unrealistic.”

items.text: Philosophy is not simply personal opinion. It asks foundational questions and requires concepts, reasons, arguments and critical examination of assumptions.

Metaphysics or ontology asks what reality is; epistemology asks what knowledge is and how it is justified; ethics asks how we should live; logic studies good reasoning; political philosophy examines authority and justice; philosophy of mind and language study consciousness, meaning and representation.

Philosophy and science overlap in rational inquiry but differ in method and level: science normally tests empirical hypotheses, while philosophy often examines concepts, presuppositions and normative questions that cannot be settled by experiment alone.

Philosophy and religion can overlap in questions of meaning, morality and ultimate reality, but philosophy typically evaluates claims through argument rather than accepting them solely on authority or revelation.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not define philosophy only as “love of wisdom” and stop. Explain its method, branches and the kinds of questions it asks.

items.text: Learn branches with one question each.
Prepare philosophy vs science vs religion as a balanced comparison.

segments.text: Argument and conceptual clarity are central.
A philosophical claim should be supported by reasons.
